Neonates of the Alabama red-bellied cooter (Pseudemys alabamensis) emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs following a developmental period that is strongly temperature-dependent. For the closely related river cooter (Pseudemys concinna), incubation at a steady 31 °C [T = 31 °C] results in hatching after approximately 55 days [ab = approximately 55 days], a duration that is likely similar for P. alabamensis given their phylogenetic proximity. At the moment of eclosion, the carapace length of these hatchlings typically measures between 25 and 31 millimeters (25-31 millimeters) [Lb = 25-31 millimeters], a modest size that reflects the substantial yolk reserves consumed during ontogeny. This initial shell dimension is critical for surviving the first weeks of life, as larger hatchlings generally exhibit higher survival rates when evading aquatic predators in the slow-moving rivers and sloughs of the Mobile Bay drainage. The transition from a yolk-dependent embryo to an actively foraging juvenile represents a period of elevated vulnerability, during which the young turtles must locate adequate basking sites and foraging grounds to support rapid somatic growth.

As juveniles progress toward adulthood, they undergo a prolonged period of maturation before reaching a terminal body size that defines the species. Under optimal conditions in the wild, adult Alabama red-bellied cooters achieve a maximum carapace length of approximately 32.25 centimeters [Li = approximately 32.25 centimeters], a dimension that distinguishes them from smaller congeners within the southeastern United States. This ultimate shell length is attained gradually over many years, reflecting the slow growth rates characteristic of long-lived freshwater turtles. Attainment of this asymptotic size typically coincides with the onset of full reproductive capability, though growth may continue at a markedly reduced pace even after sexual maturation has occurred. The relatively large body size of adult P. alabamensis likely confers advantages in terms of predator deterrence and thermoregulatory capacity, as larger individuals can retain heat more effectively during the cooler months and are less susceptible to predation by raccoons and alligators.

Reproductive output in female Alabama red-bellied cooters follows a constrained annual schedule typical of many emydid turtles. Nesting females deposit between 4 and 9 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 4 and 9 eggs per clutch], with the modal clutch size often near six eggs depending on the nutritional condition of the individual. These females produce only a single clutch of eggs each year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs each year], a reproductive frequency that limits the annual fecundity of the population but presumably benefits offspring quality by allowing greater maternal investment per egg. When maintained under controlled thermal conditions corresponding to average summer water temperatures of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], this reproductive schedule yields an output that averages about one clutch per annum [F_R_i = about one clutch per annum]. This modest annual fecundity, combined with high nest predation rates from raccoons and feral hogs, renders the species particularly vulnerable to population declines and underscores the importance of nest protection efforts in its conservation management.

Demographic traits inferred from the better-studied river cooter provide valuable comparative benchmarks for understanding the life cycle of the Alabama red-bellied cooter. Based on extrapolations from Pseudemys concinna, the time required from hatching to reach the onset of sexual maturity is approximately 6 years since birth [tp = approximately 6 years since birth] under a thermal regime of 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. This protracted juvenile period is not unusual among large-bodied emydids and reflects the considerable investment in somatic growth necessary to achieve the body size required for successful reproduction. During these pre-reproductive years, the risk of mortality remains elevated, and only a fraction of hatchlings survive to reach this critical developmental milestone. The attainment of sexual maturity does not immediately translate into annual breeding for all females, as resource availability and body condition exert additional constraints on the timing of first reproduction. Consequently, the observed age at first successful nesting in the wild may exceed the theoretical minimum time since birth at puberty.

Longevity data for the Alabama red-bellied cooter remain limited, but comparative estimates derived from its congener provide a useful approximation for population modeling. Based on records from Pseudemys concinna, the maximum lifespan of P. alabamensis is projected to be approximately 77 years [am = approximately 77 years] when maintained at an average annual temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. Such an extended lifespan, spanning many decades, has profound implications for the species' population dynamics and conservation biology. Long-lived individuals can buffer populations against occasional recruitment failures by breeding repeatedly over many seasons, a life-history strategy that is typical of species inhabiting unpredictable or seasonally variable environments. However, this same longevity also means that populations recover slowly from sustained adult mortality, making the species especially sensitive to threats such as road mortality, habitat degradation, and illegal collection. The combination of late maturity, low annual fecundity, and a long reproductive lifespan positions P. alabamensis as a classic K-selected strategist, highly dependent on the survival of older individuals for long-term population persistence.

The Alabama red-bellied cooter is predominantly herbivorous as an adult, feeding on aquatic vegetation including filamentous algae, duckweed, and submerged macrophytes in the slow-moving waters of the Mobile-Tensaw Delta. This dietary specialization influences both its growth trajectory and its spatial distribution within the watershed, as individuals concentrate in areas with abundant vegetative cover that also provides refuge from predators. Seasonal shifts in water temperature and photoperiod drive corresponding changes in foraging activity and metabolic rate, with turtles reducing their food intake substantially during the cooler winter months. These behavioral adaptations allow P. alabamensis to maintain a positive energy balance throughout the year despite the seasonal variability characteristic of subtropical climates. The species' reliance on aquatic vegetation also links its population health directly to water quality conditions, making it a potential bioindicator for assessing the ecological integrity of its limited freshwater habitat.
